name: David Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is pretty regular. Lectures in physics and maths from nine to one, problem sheets in the afternoon, and cello rehearsal with the university orchestra on Tuesday and Thursday evenings. I write everything in paper notebooks, and I keep them in order by date, which my flatmates find hilarious. I'm studying physics with the idea of becoming a secondary school teacher, and on Fridays I go home on the train to my parents' house, where my dad runs a small dental practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's probably what I expected, that technology is useful but not magic. I'd mention that people have said the same thing about calculators and computers in classrooms. I'd keep it short, because I don't love arguing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be relieved. A plateau means my plan to teach physics stays the same, and so does my slow way of doing things. I'd still be nervous about passing the training year and getting a decent school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with my notebooks, finish first year, and apply for a school volunteering scheme where you help in a maths classroom. I'd also keep playing cello, because it clears my head. I'd keep saving the small amount I earn from tutoring a neighbour's son.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. My parents pay for everything, my results are good, and teaching jobs in my area seem steady. I'd feel I'd made a sensible choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd carry on as normal. Is there anything in your own plans that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The usual teacher worries: workload, discipline, and pay. My old physics teacher looked tired by the end of every term, and a plateau doesn't make that easier, so that's what I think about when I picture teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, I told you so, probably. He thinks software tools in dentistry are mostly for booking and billing, and the real work is still done with his hands and a good light. He'd be calm about it.

say: I'd say **technology** is useful but not magic, like calculators once were.
I'd keep my comments **short**, because I don't like arguing online.
think: Privately I'm **relieved**, as my plan to teach physics stays the same.
I still fear the **training year** and finding a decent school.
do: Finish first year, keep my **notebooks**, and apply for a classroom volunteering scheme.
Keep tutoring a neighbour's son and **saving** the small earnings.
feel: **Calm**, feeling I made a sensible choice.
S0.quote: My old physics teacher looked tired by the end of every term, and a plateau doesn't make that easier, so that's what I think about when I picture teaching.
fieldNote: He pictures **teacher workload**, not AI, as his main worry in a plateau.
His calm is linked to **sensible choices** and a family cushion.
He **prefers short, careful statements** to public arguments.

steps.text: Apply for a school volunteering scheme to help in a maths classroom
Keep tutoring a neighbour's son and save the money
Carry on writing paper notes and playing cello twice a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a sensible moment to slow down and check what works before we rush into it. I'd say that teachers should be asked what they need, not told. If a friend asked me, I'd tell them to try it carefully for marking and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm uneasy. Teaching includes a lot of planning, marking and paperwork, and those are thinking tasks that could be taken over. If schools save money, there might be fewer teachers hired, which is exactly what I'm training for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a teacher I know at my old school how they plan lessons and what they use. I'd probably try one tool for marking practice papers, with a notebook beside it to compare. I'd also look up whether the training courses are changing, and when to apply.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I don't mind change, but I mind not knowing what's real. If I knew teachers would still be needed in classrooms, I'd feel much calmer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools. How would you feel if every lesson plan was drafted by one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel a bit annoyed, honestly, but I'd read through it and make changes. I'd want to be the one deciding what a child learns, not a draft I hadn't checked, but if the draft was good, I'd admit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the school do with the time saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably cut fewer corners or cut posts, and I don't know which. A head teacher I know says budgets are so tight that any saving is spent immediately. That doesn't sound hopeful for new teachers.

say: I'd say **slow down** and check what works before rushing in.
I'd say teachers should be **asked what they need**, not told.
think: Privately I'm **uneasy**: planning and marking could be taken over.
If schools save money, **fewer teachers** may be hired.
do: Ask a teacher at my old school what **tools** they use to plan.
Try one tool for **marking practice papers**, with a notebook beside it to compare.
feel: **Uneasy**, because I don't mind change but dislike not knowing what's real.
S1.quote: I'd want to be the one deciding what a child learns, not a draft I hadn't checked, but if the draft was good, I'd admit it.
fieldNote: He plans to **test one tool carefully**, a steady rather than eager approach.
He links AI savings to **teacher posts**, the heart of his worry.
He is **honest** that he would admit a good draft.

steps.text: Ask a teacher at my old school how they plan lessons
Try one AI tool for marking practice papers and compare with my notes
Check whether teacher training intakes are changing before I apply

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need clear guidance from the government, something official, with dates and plans, not rumours. I'd ask my physics department what they expect teaching to look like. I'd say it quietly, to people I trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried. If thinking AI does most mental work in two years, a lot of the reasons for a teaching degree change, including mine. I'd wonder whether children will still need teachers for anything other than company and discipline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to my parents first, then my physics tutor, and ask for honest advice. I'd stay at university for now, because leaving would feel like panic. I'd start saving more of my allowance, and ask whether my dad's practice needs help, since a dentist's hands-on work lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's the lack of time that gets me, because I like to make a plan and think things through, and two years is not a lot, so I'd lose some sleep and play more cello.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years: what's the first thing you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say the booking and billing side would change fast, but patients still need someone to look inside their mouth. Hands-on work gets about three more years, so he might be fine until around 2031. He'd still worry about the equipment costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does it mean for your dad's practice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably put the cello away for an hour and go for a long walk. Then I'd write a list of what I can control, like grades, savings and who I talk to. It sounds small, but it's the only way I get through a bad week.

say: I'd ask for **clear guidance** with dates and plans, not rumours.
I'd ask my physics department what they expect **teaching** to look like.
think: Privately I'd be **worried**: a teaching degree's value could change fast.
I'd wonder whether children need teachers for more than **company**.
do: Talk to my parents and my **physics tutor**, and stay at university for now.
Save more of my **allowance** and ask if my dad's practice needs help.
feel: **Anxious**, because two years is too little time to plan.
S2.quote: I like to make a plan and think things through, and two years is not a lot, so I'd lose some sleep and play more cello.
fieldNote: His **need to plan** drives the anxiety more than the AI itself.
He sees his father's **hands-on trade** as safer for about three years.
Staying at university is his way of **not panicking**.

steps.text: Talk to my parents and my physics tutor for honest advice
Save more of my allowance each month
Ask whether my dad's practice could use my help during holidays
Stay on the physics degree and see how schools respond

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to make a sensible plan, so let's make one. I'd write to my MP asking what the plan is for schools. I'd stay polite, and I'd ask the right questions in seminars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel anxious but able to cope. I'd finish my degree, do a teacher training year, and be teaching by about 2031, just when the robots arrive. I'd hope there'd still be classrooms and children who need human adults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree, do the training year, and in the meantime try the AI tools in a careful way so I can teach children to use them properly. I'd also start a small savings plan with my dad's help. I'd keep my options open, perhaps a masters in education.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can live with. It gives me a runway to work on, which is what I need. I'd probably stay up some nights but I'd sleep fine most of the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years: what does that room give you, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me time to change my mind slowly, which is the only way I change it. After a year of seeing it work well for others, I'd probably try one tool myself. I wouldn't be first, but I wouldn't be last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your mind about using AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not about the future, but about my own pace. I know I'm slow to adapt, and a longer timeline gives me a chance to catch up, which is what I'd tell a friend in the same position.

say: I'd say five years is long enough to **make a plan**.
I'd write to my **MP** and ask what the plan is for schools.
think: Privately I'm **anxious but coping**, hoping classrooms still need human adults.
I expect to be **teaching by 2031**, just as robots arrive.
do: Finish the degree, do the **training year**, and try AI tools carefully so I can teach children to use them.
Start a **savings plan** with my dad's help.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way I can live with.
S3.quote: I know I'm slow to adapt, and a longer timeline gives me a chance to catch up, which is what I'd tell a friend in the same position.
fieldNote: He understands his **own slowness** and uses the timeline as cover for it.
He plans to **teach children** to use AI, so his reluctance becomes a teaching idea.
He is **polite and procedural**, writing to his MP rather than protesting.

steps.text: Finish the degree and do a teacher training year
Try one AI tool carefully after seeing others use it for a year
Write to my MP asking what the plan is for schools
Start a savings plan with my dad's help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent amount of time and we should use it to get education right. I'd tell people who are panicking to breathe and make a list. I'd say it plainly, since that's how I talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm quite calm, and a bit ashamed of how calm. By then I'd be 29, with around six or seven years of teaching, and I'd be able to help children learn to use these systems well. I think a teacher who stays steady might be valuable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my degree and the training, teach for a few years, and learn the AI tools when I'm sure they're reliable. I'd probably do a masters in education part-time. I'd keep saving a small amount each month, because it's the one thing I can control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, calm in the middle. It's a feeling like knowing there's a long journey and having packed a bag. I'd get on with my cello.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is long. Do you feel any pressure at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, because ten years has a way of turning into two when you aren't paying attention. I'd check in once a year on how things are going, like a service for a car. That would keep me honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you say to someone who says the date will come sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should believe the evidence, and not the headlines either way. If the date comes sooner, I'd rather be ready than right, and a bag packed early is never wasted.

say: I'd say ten years is **decent**, and we should use it to get education right.
I'd tell panicking people to **breathe** and make a list.
think: Privately I'm **calm**, and a little ashamed of how calm.
I think a **steady teacher** might be valuable.
do: Do the degree and training, teach for a few years, and learn AI tools when they're **reliable**.
Study a **masters in education** part-time and keep saving a little.
feel: **Uneasy at the edges**, calm in the middle, like packing a bag early.
S4.quote: If the date comes sooner, I'd rather be ready than right, and a bag packed early is never wasted.
fieldNote: He feels **guilt about being calm**, which shows his conscience at work.
His idea of a **yearly check-in** is a typical careful habit.
He keeps being **reluctant** with AI until proof appears.

steps.text: Do the degree and the training year, then teach a few years
Save a small amount every month from my part-time tutoring
Check once a year how AI is changing schools before deciding more

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because I like to plan and two years doesn't leave room for a plan. What would help is somebody official telling teachers and students clearly what is changing, and in what order. I'd also want my dad's kind of small business to get help, not just the big firms.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I don't use AI tools, not even for explanations, and I know that sounds old-fashioned for 19. I just like working a problem out myself and then checking it in the textbook. Anyone can get an answer from a machine, but I want to be the teacher who can tell a child why the answer is right. If everyone around me is using them, I might have to learn eventually, but I'll want proof first.

headlineQuote: Anyone can get an answer from a machine, but I want to be the teacher who can tell a child why the answer is right.
portrait: David is 19, in his first year of **physics**, planning to teach, with strong family money and top grades.
He is centrist and resistant: he writes in notebooks and **never uses AI** until he sees proof.
He worries about change **arriving too fast** to plan, and about his dad's small business.
His mood moves with **how much notice** he gets, from calm in a plateau to anxious when the date is close.
He blames **no single group**, wants clear official guidance and relies on his family and orchestra friends.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** worries him most, because he likes to plan and two years leaves no room.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear official guidance** on what changes and in what order.
Help for **small businesses** like his dad's dental practice, not only big firms.
